chapters.title: Safety Philosophy - Why

sections.heading: Shared Responsibility
items: As an employee, you are responsible for safety of yourself and your mates
Care towards the vessel and the protection of the Environment

sections.heading: Company Safety Principles
items: No business objective will be pursued at the expense of safety
Accidents and injuries are preventable - all possible steps must be taken

sections.heading: Consequences of Unsafe Acts
items: Taking unnecessary risks is not in the Company's best interest
Unsafe actions may result in disciplinary action
A single major incident can ruin the Company and outweigh any short-term gains

chapters.title: Safety Culture - Chapter 1

sections.heading: Zero Tolerance
items: No acceptance of hazardous unsafe practices
Unsafe practices or shortcuts
Non-compliance with safety procedures

sections.heading: Proactive Approach
items: Every crew member from Master to trainee - actively spot hazards and unsafe conditions
Report errors and near misses
Vessel management must be eliminated or mitigated

sections.heading: Learning & Corrective Action
items: Analyze safety reports and feedback
Draw intelligent conclusions
Implement corrective actions promptly
Encourage enthusiasm and commitment for an incident-free operation

sections.heading: Compliance Culture
items: Applies from Top Leadership to trainee onboard
No one in a responsible position may ignore safety procedures
Compliance culture means: doing the job properly; doing it safely the first time and every time; protecting your safety and your life's safety

chapters.title: Familiarization of Ship Staff
chapters.intro: The four-section familiarization process for ship staff as per SAF-10 Booklet and SOLAS requirements.

sections.heading: Section A - Pre-Joining Briefing
items: Conducted by Company / Manning Office
Covers familiarizations and objectives
Procedures, organization structure

sections.heading: Section B - Onboard Safety Familiarization
items: Timeline: Within 24 hours of joining or before voyage begins
Conducted by: Safety Officer or designate (3/O with 6+ months rank exp. OR 2/O)
Assisted by 2/E or designate (4/E with 6+ months rank exp. OR 3/E) for machinery spaces

sections.heading: Section C - Detailed Onboard Safety (SOLAS Requirement)
items: Timeline: Within 14 days of joining
Detailed safety training to be completed
On-signer signs by signing Section C

sections.heading: Section D - Job Familiarization
items: Conducted by outgoing person or higher rank officer
Must be completed before assuming responsibility
Responsibilities & Records

sections.heading: General Requirements
items: Each crew member must read, understand & sign each section
Submit to the Master/Chief Engineer for verification & signature
A copy of last page will be filed on bridge with 3/O for records

chapters.figure: A 'Familiarization of Ship Staff' poster (ozellar MARINE) organized into Sections A-D with icons for each stage of the familiarization process.

chapters.title: SAIL - See, Act, Inform, Learn
chapters.intro: The S.A.I.L. behavioural safety observation process of four steps: See, Act, Inform, Learn.

sections.heading: 1. See (Observation)
items: Stay alert. Spot unsafe acts, hazards, or good safety practices
If it doesn't look right or feel safe, investigate - trust your instincts

sections.heading: 2. Act (Intervention)
items: Take immediate action to correct hazards or appreciate safe behavior
Intervene respectfully and stop work if danger is imminent - safety comes first

sections.heading: 3. Inform (Reporting)
items: Report what you observed and did using the S.A.I.L. form
Timely, detailed reporting helps prevent incidents and improves fleet-wide safety
It's about learning, not blame

sections.heading: 4. Learn (Prevention)
items: Analyze reports, fix root causes, and share lessons
Engage in toolbox talks and safety bulletins
What you do today can prevent tomorrow's accidents

chapters.figure: An 'S.A.I.L. - See. Act. Inform. Learn.' poster with illustrated workers depicting each of the four steps.

chapters.title: Permit to Work (PTW) System
chapters.intro: Explains the purpose, principles, authority, and compliance requirements of the Permit to Work system.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: PTW is managed on board in a variety of ways
Ensures the safety section is to provide guidance on the Permit to Work (PTW) system
Permit to Work system is to be followed

sections.heading: Key Principles
items: Procedures must be fully completed without exception before a permit is issued
PTW applies to hazardous and critical work (hot work, enclosed space entry, working aloft, electrical isolation)
Ensures risks minimized and correctives clearly define responsibilities

sections.heading: Authority & Responsibility
items: Master is overall in charge of all PTW-controlled activities but may delegate the responsibility of issuing some permits
Shore / External Authorities: In repair yards or port limits, permits may be issued by local authority, chemist, or competent authorities or legislation or repair contract
However, safety precautions as per PTW must not be compromised if local standards are lower

sections.heading: Compliance Requirement
items: At all times (except when valid local permits apply), Company's PTW system must be used

chapters.title: Isolation Procedure
chapters.intro: Purpose, triggers and key principles for isolating hazardous energy before work.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Safeguard personnel from uncontrolled release of hazardous energy
Live energy: flowing/moving (live electrical circuit, fluid in pipeline)
Stored energy: restrained (compressed spring, static pressure, stored charge)
Uncontrolled release of hazardous substances (vapours, chemicals)

sections.heading: When isolation is required
items: Work on electrical systems where contact with live connections is possible (Electrical Work Permit required, incl. HV and elevator maintenance)
Systems where automatic, remote or inadvertent activation could cause injury
Work releasing liquids/vapours from lines or pressure systems (Cold Work Permit)
Work on pressurized systems (pneumatic, hydraulic)
Work where a windmilling hazard exists (fans/impellers)

sections.heading: Key principles
items: Isolation is part of the Permit to Work (PTW) system
Controls identified from the Risk Assessment must be implemented before work begins
All residual energy sources must be neutralized
Locks and tags must be placed and clearly identified in the permit

chapters.title: LOTO - Lock Out Tag Out
chapters.intro: Lock Out Tag Out purpose, kit custody, usage guidelines and best practices.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Locks and/or tags are used to secure and identify isolation points

sections.heading: Custody & usage
items: The person in charge of the job should carry out Lock Out and Tag Out
LOTO kit kept under custody of Chief Engineer/Chief Officer
Issued to the person in charge during the Toolbox meeting
All vessels must carry out LOTO kit training using provided materials

sections.heading: Best practices
items: Keep the tagged and locked system isolated until all work is complete
Never sign off locks or tags applied by others

sections.heading: Six-step process
items: Isolate
Lock
Tag
Verify
Work
Remove

chapters.figure: Poster showing a LOTO kit (case, padlocks, hasps, tags) and a six-step icon flow.

chapters.title: Safety Officer - Role & Duties
chapters.intro: Appointment and key duties of the shipboard Safety Officer.

sections.heading: Appointment
items: Chief Engineer and Second Engineer act as Safety Officers on company-managed vessels

sections.heading: Key duties
items: Look for potential hazards and means of preventing incidents
Develop and sustain high safety consciousness among the crew
Stop unsafe practices, suggest improvements, escalate if necessary
Instruct joining seafarers in all relevant health & safety arrangements
Pair new entrants with a safety-conscious crew member
Remind experienced seamen of the importance of high safety standards
Promote safety by distributing booklets, notices and learning materials
Investigate notifiable accidents or dangerous occurrences onboard

sections.heading: Note
items: The Safety Officer is the Master's key partner in ensuring zero harm and a strong safety culture.

chapters.title: Safety Officer's Inspection Flow
chapters.intro: Step-by-step flow of the Safety Officer's periodic inspection process.

sections.heading: Inspection flow
items: Plan inspection - start of quarter, using SAF 11 A/B/C checklists
Conduct area checks - accommodation, deck, engine room, others
Record findings - use checklist, note hazards
Discuss in safety meeting - present to Master & Safety Committee
Submit to office - Superintendent's review
Follow-up in SCMM - record and track corrective actions

sections.heading: Note
items: Effective inspections are the foundation of a safer ship.

chapters.figure: Vertical flowchart connecting six inspection steps from Plan Inspection to Follow-up in SCMM.

chapters.title: Safety Meeting
chapters.intro: Requirements for convening, conducting and recording shipboard safety meetings.

sections.heading: Convening
items: Master shall convene the safety meeting at least once a month
All ship staff except watchkeepers should attend
Ideally conducted close to the end of the month

sections.heading: Superintendent presence
items: A safety meeting shall be conducted in the presence of a superintendent during his visit onboard

sections.heading: Recording minutes
items: Minutes recorded in the 'Safety meeting minutes' form
Attendees identified in the minutes
Minutes sent to office by email

sections.heading: Review
items: Review comments sent to the vessel within 1 week of submission

chapters.title: Onboard Safety Day
chapters.intro: Purpose, objectives and agenda for the monthly onboard Safety Day.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Once a month all seafarers participate in a 'Safety Day' to reinforce ownership of safety and a culture of awareness, responsibility and teamwork

sections.heading: Objectives
items: Participation of all crew members
Training & mentoring - senior officers guide juniors
Hands-on training - juniors inspect critical safety items
Open reporting culture - free reporting of hazards
Responsibility & ownership - junior ranks develop safety leadership

sections.heading: Agenda
items: Opening meeting - Master briefs crew; C/E & C/O present the plan
Incident review - discuss incidents since last Safety Day
Hazard identification - group discussions
PPE inspection - boiler suits, safety shoes, goggles, gloves, harness, fall arrestors, LOTO kits, HV equipment, work vests
Corrective actions - discuss findings and assign

sections.heading: Note
items: Safety Day is about building responsibility, awareness and ownership - not just a drill.

chapters.title: Safety Committee
chapters.intro: Composition, Safety Representative election and support for the shipboard Safety Committee.

sections.heading: Composition
items: In addition to the Master: Chief Engineer, Chief Officer, 2nd Engineer, Bosun, Cook, Engine Room Rating, Deck Department Rating
Updated list of members must be displayed on the common noticeboard

sections.heading: Safety Representative (SR)
items: Elected from the crew during the monthly Safety Committee meeting
Election presided by the Master through informal voting
Tenure 1 month, extendable; give as many crew as possible the opportunity
Danish-flag vessels: SR remains until end of service onboard
Eligibility: at least 6 months' experience on that vessel type

sections.heading: Role & support
items: The Safety Representative receives full cooperation from the Shipboard Management Team

sections.heading: Note
items: The Safety Committee ensures participation, representation and shared responsibility for safety.

chapters.title: Daily Work Plan Meeting
chapters.intro: Purpose and flow of the vessel's daily work planning meeting.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Management team (Master, C/O, C/E, 2/E) conducts a daily planning meeting to:
Plan and allocate the next day's work
Discuss ship operations, maintenance & contractor tasks
Review resources, risks and safety measures

sections.heading: Flow
items: Collect the tasks - mandatory: Master, C/O, C/E, 2/E, E/O
Officers list their own tasks; additional crew as required
Identify resources, challenges, risks; finalize tasks for next day
Crew informed of tasks; copy of task list posted in crew mess
Contractor tasks discussed with the responsible officer
Record in ADM-19 Daily Work Planner (available on Bridge & ECR)

sections.heading: Note
items: A well-planned day improves efficiency, reduces risk and ensures teamwork.

chapters.figure: Flow diagram: Collect the Task leading to Task List Final.

chapters.title: Single-Person Job Guidelines
chapters.intro: Definition, safety measures and restrictions for single-person (working-alone) jobs.

sections.heading: Definition
items: A single-person job is one done alone, without being seen or heard by others
Risk depends on the location and nature of the task

sections.heading: Safety measures
items: Limit single-person jobs - team leaders & HODs must plan to avoid them where possible
Pre-planning - discuss intended solo tasks in departmental & daily meetings
Training - team leaders must train crew on the hazards of single-person jobs
Communication - must have a reliable way to raise the alarm or contact help immediately

sections.heading: Restrictions
items: Contractors not allowed as single-person job unless a Risk Assessment is completed and the Master authorizes it
Enclosed space entry as a single-person job is prohibited

sections.heading: Note
items: Working alone increases risk - plan, inform and stay connected.

chapters.title: Smoking Policy Onboard
chapters.intro: Fire risk, designated and prohibited smoking areas, and special instructions.

sections.heading: Fire risk
items: Fire is a major hazard onboard; strict compliance with smoking rules is essential
Secret smoking is highly dangerous - risk of flammable gases in toilets, lockers or ventilation

sections.heading: Designated smoking areas
items: Officer Smoke Room and Crew Smoke Room
Controlled smoking is less risky than secret smoking - follow the rules

sections.heading: Prohibited areas
items: Navigation Bridge and Engine Control Room (ECR)
Cabins/bed, and any area during cargo/flammable operations

sections.heading: Special instructions
items: Master must ensure no smoking in wheelhouse or ECR if any duty team member objects to passive smoking
Pilots may smoke on the bridge at sea only if no flammable cargo operations and no purging/inerting/gas-freeing in progress

chapters.figure: Poster with no-smoking symbol and warning icons.

Lack of training/experience

Protect hands by use of a full boiler suit (sleeves and legs) and proper boots.
In case of chemical contact with body/eyes.

items: Secure fastening - Batteries must be properly fixed to prevent shifting in heavy weather.

Follow manufacturer's instructions unless company directs otherwise.

Disposal: Never dispose at sea; land to authorized contractors for safe disposal
Do not incinerate used batteries

Updated inventory to be maintained
All opened/in-use drums inside Paint Store always be covered with their lids
Regular and thorough safety inspections to be carried out
Lub oil storage and handling
Caustic soda handling

chapters.title: Fatigue Management
chapters.intro: IMO defines fatigue as a reduction in physical and/or mental capability from exertion.

sections.heading: Fatigue - IMO Definition
items: A reduction in physical and/or mental capability as a result of physical, mental or emotional exertion which may impair nearly all physical abilities including strength, speed, reaction making or coordination, decision making or balance.

sections.heading: Causes of Fatigue - Sleep & Rest
items: Shortage of sleep
Poor sleep quality
Insufficient rest periods between duty cycles

sections.heading: Psychological / Emotional
items: Monotony & boredom
Stress & interpersonal conflicts
Emotional strain from prolonged voyages

sections.heading: Workload Factors
items: Excessive paperwork
Work beyond normal hours (overtime, night shifts)
Boring, repetitive jobs

sections.heading: Voyage & Scheduling
items: Frequent port turnarounds
Irregular schedules & watchkeeping patterns

sections.heading: Health & Lifestyle
items: Alcohol & caffeine misuse
Poor diet and irregular eating habits

sections.heading: Port Duty Demands
items: Heavy workload during cargo ops
Limited or no shore leave

sections.heading: How to Prevent Fatigue Onboard - Sleep (The Most Effective Strategy)
items: Duration: 7-8 hours per 24 hours (minimum 6 hours continuous)
Continuity: At least 6 hours in one stretch
Quality: Deep, aligned with biological clock
Maintain pre-sleep routine (warm shower, reading, calming activities)
Ensure dark, quiet, cool, comfortable environment
Light meal before bed: avoid heavy food
Avoid stimulants: tea, coffee, colas, chocolate, alcohol-based meds (esp. 6 hours prior)
Use relaxation (yoga, meditation)

sections.heading: Rest (Apart from Sleep)
items: Breaks and activity changes to reduce strain
Rest requirement depends on: length and intensity of work before break
Duration of change of activity

sections.heading: Guidelines for Maintaining Performance
items: Get enough sleep before long duty/voyage
Ensure continuous sleep cycles, good sleep discipline

chapters.title: Practical Steps to Reduce Fatigue
chapters.intro: Practical short-term and long-term measures, plus digital wellness, to reduce fatigue onboard.

sections.heading: Temporary Relief From Fatigue
items: Allow the crew member to take a break.
Drink lots of water. Avoid caffeine.
Have a strategic nap.
Rotate the crew member to a low-risk task.
Drink lots of water.
Consider if the task can be delayed.

sections.heading: Long-Term Relief From Fatigue
items: Keep duty schedules under review.
Provide compensatory rest if needed.
Discuss fatigue during safety meetings.
Encourage open reporting of fatigue symptoms.
Schedule drills and maintenance to minimize sleep disturbance.
Develop a watchkeeping schedule for proper rest hours.
Rotate duties to balance workloads.
Transfer duties if needed during extended operations.
Maintain good shipboard living conditions.
Encourage relaxation techniques on leave.

sections.heading: Digital Wellness & Fatigue Management - Responsible Digital Device Usage
items: Limit mobile phone and laptop use at least 1 hour before bedtime
Use blue light filtering settings or apps during evening hours
Avoid high-stimulation content (social media, work emails, news) before sleep
Follow the 20-20-20 rule to reduce eye strain during prolonged screen use

sections.heading: Sleep Hygiene and Technology
items: Keep digital devices away from bed or in airplane mode during rest periods
Use do not disturb settings to prevent notifications interrupting sleep
Dim cabin lights or use warm-toned lighting during the evening
Establish a consistent pre-sleep routine that minimizes digital interaction

sections.heading: Digital Addiction Awareness
items: Monitor screen time and recognize signs of over-dependence

sections.heading: Digital Ergonomics
items: Position screens at eye level to prevent neck and back strain

sections.heading: Work / Rest Hours - General Guidance: Any 24 Hours Rule
items: Minimum 10 hrs rest in any 24 hrs
Divided into no more than 2 periods

sections.heading: Non-Conformances

sections.heading: Compensatory Rest

Retained for service period or 12 months

Store pesticides safely & handle with care

sections.heading: Health Surveillance Onboard (Purpose & Application - Sec 11A.1/1A.2) - Purpose
items: Detect early signs of ill health caused by occupational hazards
Take action before serious harm occurs
Support risk assessment & safety measures

sections.heading: Benefits

Establishes baseline health records at pre-employment

items: 20-30 min after meals
10,000 steps/day
Safety: Inform bridge watchkeeper, wear PPE

Alternate feet repeat

items: Improved stamina and suppleness
Reduced stress and better balance
Digestion
Weight control and stabilized blood sugar
Improved sleep, concentration, and self-confidence
Stronger bones and muscles, less risk of injury
Stabilized blood pressure (not during exercise), lowered cardiovascular disease risk
Fitness improves during rest, not during exercise. Avoid overstrain to prevent injuries.

chapters.title: Mental Health and Psychological Issues
chapters.intro: Mental health and wellbeing is a priority; recognize early signs and support each other.

sections.heading: Mental Health - Purpose
items: Mental Health and wellbeing will be our utmost priority. The aim is to ensure a psychologically safe, healthy, and resilient work environment.

Mental well-being is essential for building a sustainable, productive, and harmonious workplace. By taking a holistic approach, the aim is to support all stakeholders and foster an environment that promotes overall well-being.

sections.heading: Key Approaches
items: Fostering Psychological Safety: Embedding mental health into company policies and practices, creating an environment where seafarers feel valued and supported.
Empowering Through Training: Conduct regular mental health training programs to help seafarers recognize and address early signs of psychological distress.
Inclusive Mental Health Services: Ensure 24/7 access to counselling support and onboard mental health resources for seafarers, shore-based employees, and their families.
Provide Post-Incident Emotional Support: Offer structured care to help seafarers recover emotionally and maintain productivity after critical incidents.
Remember: Speak up. Seeking help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

sections.heading: Common Psychological Issues - Signs & Symptoms: Stress
items: Physical: Fatigue, trouble sleeping, headaches; High blood pressure; Digestive issues; weakened immunity and body aches
Psychological: Irritability, difficulty concentrating; Feeling overwhelmed, sadness; Sudden anger outbursts

sections.heading: Anxiety
items: Physical: Rapid heartbeat; sweating; trembling; Muscle tension; Digestive discomfort
Psychological: Excessive worry; Restlessness; Irritability
Avoiding things seen as threats, over-preparing, withdrawing socially, or engaging in compulsive actions

sections.heading: Depression
items: Physical: Chronic fatigue; Appetite or sleep changes; Unexplained aches; Slowed movements or speech
Behavioural: Substance overuse, feelings of self-care/sleeping patterns; Social withdrawal or delayed task completion

sections.heading: Suicide
items: Emotional: Hopelessness, despair; Feelings of being a burden; Loss of purpose
Physical: Neglecting hygiene; Fatigue; Changes in sleeping patterns
Warning signs: Emotive; Talking about death; withdrawing from others; risky actions; giving away belongings or sudden mood changes

sections.heading: Key Message
items: Recognize early signs. Support each other. Seeking help is strength, not weakness.

chapters.title: Psychological Safety and Self-Care Onboard
chapters.intro: Psychological safety keeps crew healthy, united, and mission-ready.

sections.heading: Psychological Safety
items: Prolonged isolation, heavy workloads, and limited support systems can lead to loneliness, fatigue, and reluctance to seek help. Addressing these challenges is crucial for maintaining mental health and operational efficiency.
Open Communication: Encourage regular sharing of concerns through casual conversations or anonymous feedback, ensuring a judgement-free environment.
Supportive Leadership: Train leaders to recognize signs of stress and provide empathetic support, including basic psychological first aid.
Confidentiality: Establish clear policies to ensure mental health discussions remain private, building trust within the team.
Wellness Check-Ins: Simple, informal check-ins can help identify early signs of distress and enable timely support.
Stigma-Free Culture: Conduct awareness activities like storytelling or myth-busting sessions to normalize discussions about mental health.

sections.heading: Self-Care Onboard - Crew Wellbeing: Physical
items: 10-min Stretch & Energize (shoulder, neck, leg, wrist)
Fitness Ladder → 10 push-ups, 15 squats, 20 step-ups

sections.heading: Emotional
items: Gratitude Postcards → weekly thank-you notes to crew
Story Circle Night → share funny or inspiring stories

sections.heading: Psychological
items: Cognitive Reframing → change negative thoughts into positive steps

sections.heading: Team Activity
items: Use downtime - music, games
Rotate leadership
Use simple resources
Keep flexible & inclusive

sections.heading: Remember
items: Self-care = safer ships, healthier crews, stronger teams

sections.heading: Keep Clear
items: Doors must not be locked/bolted without rapid means of opening from inside (no keys/tools needed)

Firefighting teams must be able to open from outside in emergencies
Escape routes/doors must never be blocked or obstructed

sections.heading: Unlock

Demonstrate door operation of external doors forming part of escape route

sections.heading: Summary

questions.explain: The HSM covers 10 permits to work.
LOTO is the Lock Out / Tag Out isolation procedure.

questions.q: What is the maximum validity of a Hot Work permit?
questions.explain: A Hot Work permit is valid for a maximum of 12 hours.

questions.q: What is the minimum rest in any 24-hour period?
questions.explain: A minimum of 10 hours rest is required in any 24 hours, in no more than 2 periods.
PPE requirements are set out in Appendix 3.

topics: Complete onboard familiarisation and uphold the safety culture.
Apply the Permit to Work system and LOTO isolation procedures.
Select and use PPE correctly as per Appendix 3.
Carry out hazard identification and risk assessment.
Manage fatigue, rest hours, health and hygiene onboard.
Support mental health and the Speak Up culture.

chapters.title: Maritime Cyber Security: Protecting the Vessel
chapters.intro: Cyber security in shipping is critical for vessel safety, environmental protection, and business continuity, distinguishing IT and OT systems and outlining Cyber Hygiene best practices.

sections.heading: IT Systems (Information Technology)
items: IT manages data (emails, servers)
Crew Welfare Wi-Fi
Network Servers
Communication (GMDSS, Inmarsat, VSAT, CCTV)
Office PCs, Email

sections.heading: OT Systems (Operational Technology)
items: OT controls physical ship functions (navigation, engines)
ECDIS, GPS, Radar
OT Failure Directly Affects Vessel Safety: A cyber-attack on systems like ECDIS, GPS, or Steering Gear can lead to immediate physical danger.
Critical Vulnerabilities: Communication systems (VSAT) and cargo systems (Loadicator) are primary targets for cyber-attacks.

sections.heading: Prevention and Incident Response
items: Practice 'Cyber Hygiene' Daily: Scan USBs before use, use strong passwords, and never share credentials.
Spot the Phishing Hook: Be wary of unknown senders, urgent requests, poor grammar, or suspicious links.
Immediate Response - Stop, Isolate, Inform: Stop using the system; Isolate it from the network; Notify the Master/DPA.

chapters.figure: Infographic cross-section of a vessel mapping IT systems (above) and OT systems (below), with a prevention/incident response panel on the right.

chapters.title: IT vs. OT: Understanding the Difference
chapters.intro: Navigating maritime cyber security means protecting both the ship (OT) and the office (IT).

sections.heading: OT: Controls the Physical World
items: Monitors and controls physical devices and processes
Real-time, time-critical response
Reboots may be unacceptable due to operational requirements
OT Requirements are Real-Time and Mission-Critical: OT response must be immediate; delays can impact ship safety and the environment
Availability is Paramount for OT

sections.heading: IT: Manages Data
items: Manages information flow
Non-real-time; consistent response
Reboots are generally acceptable

sections.heading: System Requirements Comparison
items: Performance - IT: Non-real-time, consistent response; OT: Real-time, time-critical response
Availability - IT: Reboots are generally acceptable; OT: Reboots may be unacceptable
Risk Impact - IT: Data management delays; OT: Regulatory noncompliance and physical harm

sections.heading: The 5 Pillars of Cyber Risk Management
items: Identify and Protect Critical Assets: Inventory all IT/OT software and strictly control access to authorized users only.
Detect and Respond to Incidents: Report suspected attacks to the Master or DPA immediately for escalation.
Recover and Restore Operations: Use original media for system restoration and coordinate data recovery through the Master.

chapters.title: Protecting Vessel IT and OT Systems
chapters.intro: Mapping the ship's digital infrastructure, vulnerability entry points, and the cyber incident response lifecycle.

sections.heading: Mapping the Ship's Digital Infrastructure
items: IT Supported Processes (N-Series): Manages ship administration, crew/passenger entertainment, and land-based remote IT support.
Critical OT Systems (Operational Technology): Controls essential vessel functions including propulsion, steering, navigation (ECDIS/GPS), and watertight integrity.

sections.heading: Vulnerability Entry Points
items: Open USB ports
Satellite connections
Human-error vulnerabilities in firewalls

sections.heading: The Cyber Incident Response Lifecycle
items: Phase 1: Detection & Analysis - Identify signs of tampering, malicious code implantation, or unusual system performance changes.
Phase 2: Containment & Recovery - Isolate affected systems, remove malware, and return technology to an operationally ready state.
Phase 3: Post-Incident Activity - Conduct a lessons-learned meeting and update the response plan to prevent future deficiencies.

sections.heading: Maritime Cyber Risk Formula
items: Risk = Threat x Vulnerability x Impact
Key Threats: GPS Spoofing, Malware installation, Phishing, and Sensor Freezing
Control Barriers: Two-factor authentication, network segregation, and automatic USB scanning

chapters.title: The Adversary Arsenal: Threat Profiles
chapters.intro: Six common cyber threat types facing maritime operations.

items: Malware: Viruses, Worms, and Trojans designed to infiltrate and disrupt systems.
Ransomware: Malicious code that encrypts critical ship files, accompanied by a demand for payment to unlock them.
Phishing: Fraudulent emails or websites designed to trick crew into revealing credentials or downloading payloads.
Spear Phishing: Highly personalized, targeted attacks researched and directed specifically at ship's staff or Master.
Insider Threats: Unintentional or malicious actions by crew, contractors, or vendors with physical access.
Denial of Service (DoS) & Data Theft: Overwhelming networks to crash systems or quietly exfiltrating sensitive business/crew data.

chapters.title: The Cyber Attack Lifecycle
chapters.intro: Eight sequential stages of a cyber attack against a vessel.

items: Reconnaissance: Attacker gathers data on the vessel and crew.
Intrusion: Initial breach via phishing, USB, or exposed network.
Exploitation: Triggering malware to exploit software vulnerabilities.
Privilege Escalation: Gaining administrative control over systems.
Lateral Movement: Jumping from the IT network toward the OT network.
Obfuscation: Hiding tracks to avoid antivirus detection.
Denial of Service: Disabling system functions.
Data Exfiltration: Extracting stolen information.

sections.heading: Defensive Strategy
items: Break the chain. Detecting and isolating a threat at Stage 2 prevents catastrophe at Stage 8.

chapters.figure: Horizontal timeline showing the eight attack stages

chapters.title: Deconstructing a Phishing Attempt
chapters.intro: Annotated example email highlighting the warning signs of phishing.

sections.heading: Warning Signs
items: Unknown Sender: Address slightly misspells the company name (e.g., @ozellarmarine-update.com).
Urgent Action Requested: Subject reads: URGENT: Port Clearance Document Overdue.
Unexpected Attachment: .zip or .exe file disguised as a standard PDF.
Poor Grammar: Awkwardly phrased or unprofessional sentences in the body text.
Requests for Passwords: Text asking the user to verify login credentials.
Suspicious Links: Hover-text reveals a strange URL not matching the text.

sections.heading: Key Rule
items: When in doubt: Do not click, do not download, and verify directly with the sender via phone.

chapters.figure: Mock phishing email screenshot with orange callout boxes pointing to each red flag

chapters.title: The Infection Chain Reaction: The USB Threat
chapters.intro: How a single unscanned USB device escalates into loss of safe navigation.

items: Contractor or crew inserts an unscanned USB containing hidden malware into a Crew PC.
The malware stealthily installs and searches the Shared Business Network (IT) for vulnerabilities.
The malware exploits a weak firewall port, bridging the gap and crossing into the Control Network (OT).
The malware corrupts charting data. ECDIS suddenly stops working or displays false positioning.

sections.heading: Key Rule
items: A local convenience (using an unchecked USB) directly results in the loss of safe navigation. Never bypass USB control procedures.

chapters.figure: Four-stage infographic: USB, IT network, IT/OT firewall bridge, corrupted ECDIS display

chapters.title: Recognizing an Active Breach: Incident Indicators
chapters.intro: Warning signs that indicate an active cyber breach in progress.

items: System Slowdown: Operations taking unusually long; excessive hard drive activity without prompt.
Unauthorized Access: Systems logging in autonomously; changed passwords; unknown users active.
Locked Files: Files suddenly end in strange extensions (e.g., .encrypted); ransom notes appear on desktop.
Unusual System Behavior: Mouse cursor moving on its own; pop-up windows launching; antivirus suddenly disabled.
Suspicious Communications: Massive spikes in outgoing network traffic; email system sending spam to contacts.

chapters.title: Emergency Escalation Protocol
chapters.intro: Immediate containment actions and the incident reporting chain.

sections.heading: Immediate Containment Actions
items: 1. Stop Activity: Cease using the affected system immediately.
2. Isolate: Physically disconnect the computer from the network (pull the ethernet cable, turn off Wi-Fi). Do NOT turn off the power.
3. Preserve: Leave the screen as is to preserve digital evidence.
4. Await Guidance: Do not attempt to fix or run unauthorized scans.

sections.heading: Incident Reporting Chain
items: Crew Member
Master (Ship's Cyber Security Officer)
DPA (Designated Person Ashore / Company Cyber Security Officer)
IT Team
Emergency Response Team

chapters.figure: Reporting-chain flow diagram alongside four containment-action cards

chapters.title: Cyber Defense Is Modern Seamanship
chapters.intro: Closing message framing cyber defense as core to safe seamanship.

items: The digitalization of the maritime industry brings unprecedented efficiency, but it requires a new standard of vigilance.
Protecting the digital systems of this vessel is no different than maintaining a watertight seal or standing a sharp navigational watch.
By identifying threats, securing your perimeter, and responding rapidly to incidents, you ensure the safety of the crew, the cargo, and the ship.

sections.heading: Key Message
items: Vigilance is our strongest firewall. Safe, secure, and uninterrupted operations rely on you.

sections.heading: Vulnerable Ship Systems
items: ECDIS Navigation Systems
GPS / AIS Positioning Systems
GMDSS / VSAT Communication Systems

sections.heading: Think Before You Click
items: Unknown Email?
Unverified USB?
Suspicious Link?
Unauthorized Device?
STOP • THINK • VERIFY

sections.heading: Every Crew Member Is a Cyber Defender
items: Protect Passwords: Use strong passwords and change them regularly.
Use Approved Software Only: Install software only if approved by the company.
Verify Emails: Check sender carefully before opening any email or attachment.
Scan USB Devices: Scan all removable media before use.
Never Share Credentials: Keep your login details private.
Report Suspicious Activity: Report anything unusual immediately.

sections.heading: Common Cyber Threats
items: Phishing Emails: Fraudulent emails to steal information.
Malware & Viruses: Malicious software that can damage systems.
Ransomware: Locks your data and demands payment.
Fake Websites: Deceptive websites to steal credentials.
Unauthorized USB Devices: Malicious devices can infect ship systems.
Unsecured Remote Access: Unauthorized access can compromise systems.

sections.heading: If You Suspect a Cyber Incident
items: 1. STOP: Stop using the affected system.
2. INFORM THE MASTER: Inform the Master immediately.
3. ISOLATE THE SYSTEM: Disconnect from network if safe.
4. REPORT TO OFFICE / DPA: Report to the Office or DPA without delay.
5. PRESERVE EVIDENCE: Do not delete or change anything.

sections.heading: Remember
items: One Email, One USB Device, One Mobile Phone, One Unsafe Connection CAN AFFECT THE ENTIRE SHIP.
Cyber Security Is Everyone's Responsibility: STOP • THINK • VERIFY • REPORT.
Protect People, Protect the Ship, Protect the Cargo, Protect the Environment.
